items.claim: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has the authority to apply the collateral source rule when awarding past pecuniary damages against a federal agency under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), allowing it to decline to deduct insurance benefits received by a claimant through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.
items.citation: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's Use of the Collateral Source Rule in Federal Sector Discrimination Cases
items.case_name: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's Use of the Collateral Source Rule in Federal Sector Discrimination Cases
items.case_holding_text: When the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission awards past pecuniary damages against a federal agency pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), it may apply the collateral source rule to decline to deduct insurance benefits that a claimant received through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.
items.source_text_used: When the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission awards past pecuniary damages against a federal agency pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), it may apply the collateral source rule to decline to deduct insurance benefits that a claimant received through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.claim: Temporal proximity between protected activity and termination does not establish a causal connection when there is evidence of intervening performance concerns.
items.case_holding_text:
we conclude that the trial court did not err when it found that there is

no genuine issue of material fact whether there was a causal connection between Ms. Whitney’s

protected activity and her termination. Although Ms. Whitney told the CEO about her concerns

with the compliance department only a couple of months before her termination, the CEO

concluded in his initial report that she should not be terminated. Only after he received additional

information, which did not include any additional allegations from Ms. Whitney, did he decide to
                                                   13


terminate her. As this Court noted in Lindsay, temporal proximity does not establish a causal

connection if there is evidence of intervening performance concerns. Lindsay, 2009-Ohio-1216,

at ¶ 13 (9th Dist.). Ms. Whitney’s second assignment of error is overruled.

                                 ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR III

       THE TRIAL COURT ERRED BY OVERLOOKING, WEIGHING AND OR
       FAILING TO CREDIT EVIDENCE IN REJECTING WHITNEY’S CAT’S PAW
       THEORY OF LIABILITY.

       {¶28} In her third assignment of error, Ms. Whitney argues that the trial court incorrectly

rejected her cat’s paw theory of liability. “A ‘cat’s paw’ is a person used by another to accomplish

the other’s purposes.” Smith v. Ohio Dept. of Pub. Safety, 2013-Ohio-4210, ¶ 55 (10th Dist.),

citing EEOC v. BCI Coca–Cola Bottling Co., 450 F.3d 476, 484 (10th Cir. 2006). Under this

theory, even if the person who made an adverse employment decision was unbiased, if a lower-

level supervisor had a retaliatory animus, the employer may be held liable. “The plaintiff must

show[,]” however, “that the lower-level supervisor’s discriminatory animus was a ‘but-for’ cause

of, or a determinative influence on, the unbiased superior’s adverse employment decision.” Id. at

¶ 62. Influence by a lower-level supervisor that was merely a motivating factor to the adverse

employment action is insufficient. Id. at ¶ 61.

       {¶29} Ms. Whitney argues that the trial court failed to recognize evidence in her favor.

She argues that the chief legal officer significantly altered the scope of the investigation being

carried out by outside counsel, including having it focus on the employee relations department’s

handling of IS complaints. She argues that the chief legal officer also requested that outside

items.claim: The Court of Claims dismissed the breach of contract claim based on a collective bargaining agreement for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
items.case_holding_text: The Court of Claims did not err in granting Ohio State University's ("OSU") motion for summary judgment on the employment discrimination claim or in dismissing the breach of contract claim based on a collective bargaining agreement for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
items.source_text_used: The Court of Claims did not err in granting Ohio State University's ("OSU") motion for summary judgment on the employment discrimination claim or in dismissing the breach of contract claim based on a collective bargaining agreement for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

items.claim: An employer's use of subjective performance evaluations, when applied inconsistently across protected and non-protected employee groups, may constitute sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent under Title VII. The Second Circuit held that statistical disparities in evaluation outcomes, combined with supervisor discretion unchecked by objective criteria, can survive summary judgment in an employment discrimination claim.
items.citation: Delgado v. Harwick Manufacturing Corp., 883 F.3d 214 (2nd Cir. 2020)

items.claim: An employer's use of facially neutral scheduling policies that disproportionately burden employees of a protected religious class constitutes disparate impact discrimination under Title VII. The court held that the employer must demonstrate a compelling operational necessity before such policies may be enforced without reasonable accommodation.
items.citation: Bellworth v. Meridian Transit Authority, 638 F.2d 214 (D.C. Cir. 1981)

items.claim: An employer's facially neutral shift-reassignment policy may constitute actionable disparate impact discrimination under Title VII when statistical evidence demonstrates that the policy disproportionately displaces employees of a protected racial class from higher-wage positions. The court held that plaintiffs need not prove discriminatory intent when such statistical disparity is both substantial and causally linked to the specific employment practice challenged.
items.citation: Dellworth v. Cascade Manufacturing Group, Inc., 138 F.3d 512 (4th Cir. 1997)
items.case_name: Dellworth v. Cascade Manufacturing Group, Inc.
